cc: Back pain with new bladder difficulty and leg symptoms

HPI: 27-year-old woman with low back pain beginning 3 days ago after lifting a heavy box; urinary difficulty began 6 hours ago. Deep severe pain, 8/10, shoots down the backs of both legs and worsens with bending/coughing. Leg symptoms and bladder difficulty are new today. Numbness between the legs when wiping, subjective weakness in both feet and full-bladder sensation with only drops passed. Lying still and ibuprofen 400 mg twice provided little relief. Prior strains resolved without urinary symptoms; this episode differs.

Perspective: Can I just get my back adjusted?

PMH: Previous mechanical back pain; no cancer, diabetes or immune suppression.

PSH: No spine surgery or recent procedures.

Meds: Ibuprofen 400 mg twice today; no anticoagulants.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No injection or other recreational drug use. Warehouse supervisor; lives with husband.

FH: Mother hypertension; father healthy; brother healthy; no known hereditary neurologic illness.

ROS: Neurologic - Reports back pain. Reports saddle numbness. Reports leg weakness. Urinary - Reports retention. Denies dysuria. Denies hematuria. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies weight loss.
Reproductive history: I do not think I am pregnant, but I have not taken a pregnancy test.
Reproductive history: My last period was 2 weeks ago.
note.O:
Vitals: T 98.6 F oral, P 92 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and uncomfortable, moving cautiously.
Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.
Lungs: In the examined posterior fields, clear breath sounds bilaterally.
Abdomen: Suprapubic fullness and discomfort on gentle palpation.
Musculoskeletal: Lower lumbar paraspinal tenderness.
Musculoskeletal: Bilateral ankle dorsiflexion 4/5; proximal leg strength 5/5.
Neurologic: Reduced light touch along the lateral feet bilaterally.
Neurologic: Achilles reflexes reduced bilaterally; patellar reflexes preserved.
Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
A: 1. Cauda equina compression from lumbar disc herniation
P: 1. Transfer to the emergency department immediately for spine assessment and urgent lumbar MRI; document exact onset of bladder and saddle symptoms and assess motor/sensory deficits without delaying transfer; explain possible nerve compression and need for urgent specialist decisions; avoid spinal manipulation or a routine wait-and-see plan.

2. Review fever, injection drug use, immune suppression and procedures; obtain urgent lumbar MRI and infection testing through the emergency team if indicated; explain that lack of fever alone cannot exclude serious spinal infection.

3. Ask cancer and constitutional history and obtain urgent imaging for neurologic compression; involve the relevant spine/oncology teams if supported; explain that malignancy is a possibility to assess, not a known result.

cc: Back pain with new bladder difficulty and leg symptoms

HPI: 27-year-old woman with low back pain beginning 3 days ago after lifting a heavy box; urinary difficulty began 6 hours ago. Numbness between the legs when wiping, subjective weakness in both feet and full-bladder sensation with only drops passed. Lying still and ibuprofen 400 mg twice provided little relief. Prior strains resolved without urinary symptoms; this episode differs.

P: 1. Transfer to the emergency department immediately for spine assessment and urgent lumbar MRI; document exact onset of bladder and saddle symptoms and assess motor/sensory deficits without delaying transfer; explain possible nerve compression and need for urgent specialist decisions; avoid spinal manipulation or a routine wait-and-see plan. Use a brief nerve-to-bladder explanation, check understanding and explain why urgent assessment takes priority over manipulation.

2. Review fever, injection drug use, immune suppression and procedures; obtain urgent lumbar MRI and infection testing through the emergency team if indicated; explain that lack of fever alone cannot exclude serious spinal infection.

3. Ask cancer and constitutional history and obtain urgent imaging for neurologic compression; involve the relevant spine/oncology teams if supported; explain that malignancy is a possibility to assess, not a known result.
